name: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk
info: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk (c. 1881–1938) was an Ottoman officer who led the Turkish War of Independence, founded the Republic of Turkey and, as its first president from 1923 to 1938, imposed sweeping secular reforms under one-party rule.

facts.born: c. 1881 in Salonica (Selanik), Ottoman Empire, as Mustafa; son of Ali Rıza Efendi, a military officer, title deed clerk and lumber trader, and Zübeyde Hanım; a Muslim, Turkish-speaking family that Andrew Mango calls precariously middle-class
facts.died: 10 November 1938 at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul, aged 57, of cirrhosis; laid to rest in the Ethnography Museum of Ankara and moved to the mausoleum of Anıtkabir in 1953
facts.role: Ottoman army officer (from 1905); commander of the 19th Division at Gallipoli; leader of the Turkish National Movement and speaker of the Grand National Assembly (from 1920); commander in chief (1921), field marshal and Gazi; founder of the People's Party (1923); first president of the Republic of Turkey (1923–1938)
facts.known: the Defence of Gallipoli; the Turkish War of Independence; founding the Republic of Turkey (1923); abolishing the sultanate and the caliphate; the Latin-based Turkish alphabet (1928); equal civil and political rights for women; Kemalism and its Six Arrows; the one-party state and Turkification

t: An Ottoman officer from Salonica who rose to prominence at Gallipoli, Mustafa Kemal led the Turkish National Movement against the partition of the country after the First World War and won a victory confirmed in the Treaty of Lausanne of 1923.

As first president of the Republic of Turkey from 1923 to 1938 he abolished the caliphate, closed the religious courts and orders, introduced a secular civil code and the Latin-based alphabet, and gave women equal civil and political rights.

He ruled a one-party state that suppressed its opponents and pressed minorities such as the Kurds to assimilate; praised as a nation-builder and an inspiration to anti-colonial movements, he is also condemned for repression and for continuing the persecution of Christian minorities begun by the CUP.
dyk: When Mustafa Kemal asked linguists in 1928 how long a new Latin-based alphabet would take to introduce, most said three to five years; he is said to have answered, "We shall do it in three to five months." The alphabet was introduced on 1 November 1928.
ev: Born Mustafa in Salonica, in the Ottoman Empire, to Ali Rıza Efendi and Zübeyde Hanım
The Ottoman Empire enters the First World War, a step he thought a fatal mistake; at Gallipoli he commands the 19th Division and holds his position until the Allies retreat
Lands at Samsun on 19 May to organise a national movement against the occupation and issues the Amasya Circular
As commander in chief defeats the Greek army at the Battle of the Sakarya and is made field marshal and Gazi
The Treaty of Lausanne is signed and the Republic of Turkey is proclaimed, with him as its first president
The caliphate is abolished and its powers transferred to the Grand National Assembly; sharia courts are closed
Introduces the Latin-based Turkish alphabet and abolishes the use of the Arabic script
Dies of cirrhosis at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul and is succeeded by İsmet İnönü

sections.early:
Mustafa Kemal was born in Salonica (Selanik), in the Ottoman Empire, around 1881. His parents were Ali Rıza Efendi, a military officer, title deed clerk and lumber trader, and Zübeyde Hanım, born to a farming family in Langaza; of his siblings only his sister Makbule survived childhood. According to Andrew Mango the family was Muslim, Turkish-speaking and precariously middle-class; claims about his ancestry vary widely, and Islamist opponents disturbed by his reforms later claimed he had Jewish Dönme ancestors. He was born Mustafa. The origin of the name Kemal is uncertain: some say a mathematics teacher gave it to him, while Mango suggests he may have chosen it himself in tribute to the nationalist poet Namık Kemal.

His mother sent him briefly to a religious school; at his father's direction he moved to the Şemsi Efendi School, which had a more secular curriculum. His father died when he was seven. Against his mother's wish that he learn a trade, he took the entrance exam for the Salonica Military School in 1893, went on in 1896 to the Monastir Military High School, where he excelled at mathematics, and entered the Ottoman Military Academy in 1899. He graduated from the Ottoman Military College in Constantinople on 11 January 1905. Shortly afterwards he was arrested for his activities against the regime of Sultan Abdul Hamid II and held for several months.
sections.rise:
Posted to Damascus, Mustafa Kemal joined a secret society of reformist officers and then the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP), though he later became known for criticising its leaders. He helped suppress the counter-revolution of April 1909 and depose Abdul Hamid II. In the Italo-Turkish War he commanded the Ottoman forces at Derna, and in the Balkan Wars he took part in the recovery of Edirne in 1913. He thought the Ottoman entry into the First World War in 1914 a fatal mistake. At Gallipoli he commanded the 19th Division, became the front-line commander after correctly anticipating where the Allies would attack, and held his position until they retreated; later he fought in the Caucasus and Palestine, and Lord Kinross wrote that he was the only Turkish general in the war who never suffered a defeat.

After the Armistice of Mudros the Allies occupied Constantinople and İzmir. Sent to Anatolia as an army inspector, Mustafa Kemal reached Samsun on 19 May 1919, issued the Amasya Circular declaring the country's independence in danger, resigned from the army and led the congress at Sivas. On 23 April 1920 the Grand National Assembly opened in Angora (Ankara) with him as speaker, and on 12 May a court-martial of the rival government sentenced him to death in absentia. Rejecting the Treaty of Sèvres, which partitioned the Ottoman Empire, he raised a national army to fight the Armenians in the east and the Greeks in the west, supplied with gold and arms by the Bolshevik government.
sections.deeds:
Made commander in chief in August 1921, Mustafa Kemal defeated the Greeks at the Sakarya and was made field marshal and Gazi; in August 1922 he broke the Greek lines at Dumlupınar, and Turkish forces retook İzmir on 9 September. The Treaty of Lausanne of 24 July 1923 recognised the Assembly as the government of Turkey, and on 29 October 1923 the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed with him as its first president.

The sultanate had been abolished in 1922; on 3 March 1924 the caliphate followed, and sharia courts were closed in April. A unified school system was created, the Hat Law of 1925 replaced the fez with Western-style hats, and Sufi orders and lodges were closed. In 1926 a penal code modelled on Italy's and a civil code modelled on Switzerland's gave women equality with men in inheritance and divorce. On 1 November 1928 he introduced the Latin-based Turkish alphabet, and literacy rose from 10.6% in 1927 to 22.4% in 1940. Women gained full political rights in 1934, the year the Surname Law gave him the name Atatürk. State enterprises, banks and railways were founded, the French tobacco monopoly was taken over by the state, and the first five-year plan was put in place. Abroad, under the motto "Peace at home, peace in the world", he made peace with Greece, negotiated the Balkan Pact and regained control of the Straits at Montreux in 1936.
sections.opponents:
Mustafa Kemal belonged to the CUP, which initiated and implemented the Armenian genocide, but he was not directly involved in it, and how far he criticised or supported it has been debated. In speeches for domestic audiences he presented Turks as innocent and as victims of Armenian atrocities. The nationalists relied on the support of perpetrators of the genocide and made the return of Armenian survivors impossible, and his followers expelled or murdered many Christians from Anatolia. Nearly 100,000 Armenians were massacred in Transcaucasia by the Turkish army, and the ethnic cleansing of Armenians and Greeks from Anatolia was largely completed through massacres, flight, expulsions and the population exchange with Greece.

By the mid-1920s his opponents had been suppressed and a one-party regime cemented around him. The Sheikh Said Rebellion of 1925 was put down under emergency law, the Progressive Republican Party was dissolved, and after a plot to assassinate him in 1926 several surviving CUP leaders were hanged, in an investigation used to undermine opponents of his reforms. Communists were arrested in 1927. Turkification campaigns such as "Citizen speak Turkish!", the Surname Law and the renaming of places pressed minorities to assimilate. According to the Turkish general Osman Pamukoğlu, he personally gave the operational order of the Dersim massacre (1937–1938). Critics denounce him as an authoritarian despot; his biographer Mango argues that his "enlightened authoritarianism left a reasonable space for free private lives".
sections.last:
A second experiment with opposition, the Liberal Republican Party founded at his request by Fethi Okyar in August 1930, became a centre of opposition to his reforms and was dissolved by its founder that November. Atatürk founded the Turkish Language Association and the Turkish Historical Society in 1931 and personally oversaw the Sun Language Theory, which held that all human languages descended from one Central Asian primal language. In the late 1930s his turn towards Britain and the Hatay issue strained relations with his long-time prime minister İsmet İnönü, and in 1937 he made Celâl Bayar prime minister. He had married Latife Uşşaki in 1923 and divorced her in 1925, and he adopted thirteen children, among them Sabiha Gökçen, Turkey's first female pilot.

For most of his life he was a moderate-to-heavy drinker, often taking half a litre of rakı a day, and he smoked. His health worsened during 1937, and in early 1938 he fell seriously ill; in Istanbul he was diagnosed with cirrhosis. He died at Dolmabahçe Palace on 10 November 1938, aged 57, and İnönü succeeded him as president. 17 countries sent special representatives to the funeral. His remains lay in the Ethnography Museum of Ankara until 1953, when they were moved to the mausoleum of Anıtkabir. He left his possessions to the Republican People's Party, providing for his sister Makbule and his adopted children.
sections.legacy:
Atatürk's policies and ideas became known as Kemalism, summed up in the Six Arrows. He has been praised for his military accomplishments, nation-building, reforms and diplomacy, and he inspired anti-colonial and anti-imperialist movements: Jawaharlal Nehru, Habib Bourguiba and Anwar Sadat revered him, and the All-India Muslim League eulogised him on his death. Many of his reforming ideas were already common in Ottoman intellectual circles. A lasting multi-party system came only in 1945, and in 1950 his party lost its majority.

His personality cult and the Kemalist historiography that grew around it have had a significant and continuing influence on Turkey's political culture. His portrait is in public buildings and schools and on all Turkish lira banknotes, and at 9:05 am every 10 November most people in the streets pause for a minute at the time of his death. A law of 1951 outlawed insults to his memory; Reporters Without Borders argued in 2010 that such laws contradict European Union standards of free speech. The United Nations and UNESCO marked the centenary of his birth in 1981.

Assessments remain divided. To the Allies during the war of independence he was a "bandit chief", and Arthur Balfour called him the "most terrible of all the terrible Turks". H. C. Armstrong's biography of 1932, the first published in his lifetime, compared him to Timur and Genghis Khan. He has been condemned for the one-party state, for assimilationist policies against minorities such as the Kurds and for continuing the persecution of Christian minorities begun by the CUP.

summary: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk (c. 1881–1938) was an Ottoman officer who led the Turkish War of Independence and founded the Republic of Turkey, serving as its first president from 1923 until his death. His secular reforms reshaped law, education, dress and the alphabet, while his one-party rule suppressed opponents and pressed minorities to assimilate.

notes: Birth: the article gives only c. 1881; start 1881, circa true. His age at death is given as 57.
Gallipoli: the article gives no year for the battle, so the 1914 event is dated by the Ottoman entry into the war and Gallipoli is told without a year.
Latife's surname: the Personal life section spells it Uşşaki, the dress section Uşaklıgil; Uşşaki is used.
The 12 May 1920 death sentence: the article says 'by the Turkish courts-martial' amid the power struggle between the two governments; the section says 'a court-martial of the rival government'.
Conservative Muslim criticism of his secularism is in the 'opponents'-type lead of the article; cut from 'legacy' for length.

The Liberal Republican Party: the article says it was founded on 11 August 1930 and dissolved in November 1930, and mentions the Menemen Incident of 23 December 1930 in the same passage (an apparent order problem in the article); the Menemen Incident is left out.
The article credits the Kemalist economy with GDP figures ('on par with Japan') and 150% industrial growth without attribution; left out.
The article's claims about the Kemalist labour participation rate (70%) are unsourced in the text; left out.

The Great Soviet Encyclopedia's 1953 criticism, the Mosul question, Hatay's accession in 1939, Dimitrina Kovacheva and Fikriye Hanım, and the debate over his religious beliefs (agnostic, deist or atheist by various sources) were left out for space.
The 1934 political rights for women: the article dates the move to 5 December 1934.
